clinicalPearls: A true ocular emergency in which immediate, copious irrigation takes priority over history-taking and detailed examination

Alkali burns are generally more damaging than acid burns because alkalis penetrate tissues rapidly by liquefactive necrosis, whereas acids cause coagulative necrosis that tends to limit deeper penetration
Irrigation should continue until the tear film pH returns to neutral, and the fornices must be swept and everted to remove any retained particulate matter (e.g. lime or cement)
The degree of limbal ischaemia (blanching) and corneal clarity are the key prognostic signs, forming the basis of grading systems such as Roper-Hall and Dua
A deceptively white, non-injected eye after an alkali burn can indicate severe limbal ischaemia rather than a mild injury
Later management principles aim to promote epithelial healing, control inflammation with topical steroids, prevent infection, support the ocular surface, and control intraocular pressure
Severe burns can be complicated by limbal stem cell deficiency, symblepharon, corneal melting and perforation, glaucoma, and eventual scarring
Bilateral injury and workplace or assault-related exposures require attention to both eyes and appropriate safeguarding and occupational follow-up
reference.pathophysiology: Chemical injury damages the ocular surface through direct chemical action on cells and the extracellular matrix. Alkalis dissolve cell membrane lipids and penetrate deeply by liquefactive necrosis, reaching the anterior chamber and damaging the limbal stem cells, corneal stroma, trabecular meshwork, and intraocular structures. Acids denature and precipitate proteins, producing coagulative necrosis that can form a barrier limiting deeper spread, though strong acids still cause severe injury. Destruction of limbal stem cells impairs corneal epithelial regeneration, leading to persistent epithelial defects, conjunctivalisation, and scarring, while ischaemia and inflammation predispose to stromal melting and perforation.
additionalDifferentials: Thermal burn of the ocular surface
Ultraviolet or radiation keratitis (e.g. welder's flash)
Severe infective keratitis or corneal ulcer
additionalInvestigations: Measurement of ocular surface pH before and after irrigation to guide continued irrigation
Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein to assess epithelial defect size and corneal clarity
Assessment and grading of limbal and conjunctival ischaemia
Intraocular pressure measurement, as burns can cause acute and chronic pressure rise
Eyelid eversion and fornix inspection for retained particulate chemical
redFlags: Any chemical exposure requires immediate copious irrigation before other assessment, as delay worsens outcome
Extensive limbal blanching/ischaemia and a hazy or opaque cornea indicating a severe, sight-threatening burn
A deceptively white, quiet eye masking severe ischaemic damage after alkali injury
Rising intraocular pressure, corneal melting, or threatened perforation requiring urgent specialist care
reference.prognosis: Prognosis correlates closely with the initial extent of limbal ischaemia and corneal opacification; mild burns with minimal limbal involvement usually heal well, whereas severe burns with extensive limbal stem cell loss risk chronic surface failure, scarring, and permanent visual loss despite intensive treatment. Prompt and thorough irrigation is the single most important factor improving outcome.
pitfalls: Delaying irrigation to complete history or examination first
Stopping irrigation before the pH has normalised or failing to check pH
Not everting the lids and sweeping the fornices, leaving retained caustic particles
Underestimating a white, non-inflamed eye that actually reflects severe limbal ischaemia
management: Immediate and copious irrigation continued until the tear-film pH returns to neutral, with eyelid eversion and sweeping of the fornices to remove retained particulate such as lime or cement, taking priority over history and examination
Promote epithelial healing with intensive lubrication, a bandage contact lens and ascorbate or citrate therapy, and autologous serum drops in severe surface failure
Control inflammation with topical corticosteroids in the early phase, adding cycloplegia for comfort
Prevent secondary infection with topical antibiotics
Control raised intraocular pressure with antiglaucoma medication
Grade limbal ischaemia and corneal clarity and monitor closely for stromal melting and perforation
Surgical intervention for severe injury, including amniotic membrane transplantation, limbal stem cell grafting and tarsorrhaphy
Urgent and ongoing ophthalmology involvement to guide staged surface rehabilitation
